agency: Alaska Department of Health (DOH), Division of Public Assistance (DPA)
admin_note: Alaska is a STATE-ADMINISTERED SNAP program — DPA processes all SNAP cases centrally (no borough/municipal policy authority), structurally similar to this roster's Delaware, Nebraska, Connecticut, and other centrally-administered packs. GENUINE STRUCTURAL FLAGSHIP FINDING (matches this task's own framing, and confirms it rather than requiring a correction): Alaska's SNAP program is NOT simply divided into two contiguous-48-style zones. Its FY2026 income-eligibility table (four columns: 130% FPL gross, 100% FPL net, 165% FPL elderly/disabled-separate-household, and 200% FPL BBCE) is statewide and does not vary by zone at all — the zone split (Urban / Rural I / Rural II) applies ONLY to maximum-allotment dollar amounts and minimum-benefit floors, a structurally DIFFERENT axis than income eligibility. A SECOND, entirely SEPARATE zone system — six named heating-utility regions (Central, Northern, Northwest, South Central, Southeastern, Southwestern) — governs the Standard Utility Allowance and non-heating utility standards (electricity, telephone, sewer, water), each independently dollar-valued and NOT aligned 1:1 with the Urban/Rural I/Rural II allotment zones. This pack fetched Alaska DOH's own current 'Alaska SNAP Standards' PDF (dated 8/29/2025, effective 10/1/2025) directly and confirms all three axes (income limits statewide; allotments by 3 zones; utility allowances by 6 heating regions) rather than assuming a single shared zone table, which several secondary/aggregator sources this pack found do NOT distinguish. SECOND FLAGSHIP FINDING (recent, dateable state policy change several older secondary sources may not reflect): Alaska adopted Broad-Based Categorical Eligibility (BBCE) only recently — DPA's own BBCE FAQ (dated 06/26/25) confirms BBCE applies to SNAP households that apply or recertify ON OR AFTER JULY 1, 2025, raising the gross-income gate to 200% FPL for most households; this is NOT a longstanding Alaska policy, and this pack flags that any secondary source describing Alaska SNAP using only the older 130%/100% FPL two-column structure (with no 200% BBCE column) is very likely working from pre-July-2025 information. THIRD FLAGSHIP FINDING (primary-source confirmation of a minority-position, modified-ban structure, reached by chasing the statute directly rather than accepting DPA's own FAQ language at face value): DPA's own BBCE FAQ lists a household with a member 'Convicted after 08/22/96 of a federal or state felony for possession, use or distribution of illegal drugs' as one of several categories EXCLUDED from BBCE — read alone, this could be misread as Alaska applying the unmodified federal lifetime drug-felony SNAP ban. This pack instead fetched the underlying statute, AS 47.27.015, directly (via cross-corroborated FindLaw/Justia/CLASP text after a direct HTTP 403 on law.justia.com and codes.findlaw.com) and confirms Alaska's ban is MODIFIED, not absolute: a person convicted after 8/22/1996 of a qualifying drug felony is disqualified from SNAP UNLESS they demonstrate to DPA's satisfaction that they are satisfactorily serving or have completed probation/parole, are in or have completed mandatory drug/alcohol treatment, have taken action toward rehabilitation (including treatment participation), or are complying with a reentry plan — a conditional carve-out structurally similar to this roster's Hawaii, Nebraska, and Kentucky findings. Being excluded from BBCE for this reason does not mean permanent SNAP exclusion; it means the household must clear AS 47.27.015's rehabilitation-pathway conditions AND the standard (non-BBCE) income/resource test. FOURTH FINDING, TOOLING/LEGACY-MIRROR TRAP CAUGHT: this pack found and explicitly avoided relying on dpaweb.hss.state.ak.us, Alaska's old RoboHelp-generated SNAP policy manual — it returns clean HTTP 200 with no error signal, but its own broadcast/addendum index shows no update newer than December 2021, meaning it predates BBCE (7/2025), OBBBA's ABAWD age changes (11/2025), and at least four annual COLA cycles; this pack used it ONLY for one narrow, believed-stable structural feature (the PFD Hold Harmless mechanism, cross-corroborated against DPA's live consumer page's own PFD cross-reference) and does not cite it for any dollar figure. FIFTH FINDING, internal inconsistency WITHIN Alaska's own live, currently-served site (not an archived snapshot): this pack fetched two DOH pages on the same date (2026-08-12) and found them in direct conflict on the ABAWD age range — the general SNAP consumer page states the pre-OBBBA range 'between the ages of 18 and 54,' while DOH's own dedicated 'H.R. 1 - AK Impacts' FAQ page states the current, correct post-11/1/2025 OBBBA range of 18-64 explicitly. This pack treats the H.R. 1 FAQ page as authoritative for ABAWD age, since it directly addresses the OBBBA transition the general page has not yet been updated to reflect. SIXTH FINDING: Alaska currently has an ACTIVE, unusually broad ABAWD time-limit waiver — FNS approved a 'Good Faith Exemption' waiver effective 11/1/2025 through 10/31/2026 covering every Alaska census area and borough EXCEPT the Municipality of Anchorage, confirmed directly from DOH's own H.R. 1 FAQ page — a materially different, more favorable status than this roster's Delaware pack (no active waiver) and consistent with this roster's Hawaii pack's own observation that Alaska (unlike Hawaii) has an active waiver under the noncontiguous-state 1.5x-national-unemployment threshold. Confirm current operative practice with the applicant's own local DPA office — the same caution this roster already carries for every other state built so far.
system: DPA processes SNAP centrally through the Alaska Connect Portal (accessed via a MyAlaska account at my.alaska.gov) and Alaska's Resource for Integrated Eligibility Service (ARIES) self-service system; applicants without email access can use a paper Application for Services, and in-person help is available at DPA field offices statewide. The Virtual Contact Center (1-800-478-7778) handles phone applications and case changes. Once every six months, active SNAP recipients must complete a SNAP Interim Report via the portal; the Elderly Simplified Application Project (ESAP) offers a simplified, 36-month certification period for households where all adults are 60+ or disabled. Alaska is one of only two states (with Hawaii) authorized to request ABAWD time-limit waivers at a lower, noncontiguous-state-specific unemployment threshold (1.5x the national average, versus the mainland's flat 10% floor), and currently has an active statewide waiver excluding only the Municipality of Anchorage (see admin_note). Alaska also runs a SNAP feature this pack found no equivalent for elsewhere in this roster: eligible households in communities with limited retail-store access who rely substantially on subsistence hunting and fishing may use a specially designated SNAP ID card to buy hunting/fishing equipment (nets, lines, hooks, rods, harpoons, knives, ice augers) — not firearms, ammunition, clothing, shelter, or transportation items — with SNAP benefits, per a signed subsistence hunting and fishing statement filed at application (see subsistence-hunting-fishing supplement).

This pack also deliberately tested dpaweb.hss.state.ak.us, Alaska's old RoboHelp-generated policy manual, BEFORE trusting any of its content: it returns a clean HTTP 200 with no WAF or error signal of any kind, which is exactly the legacy-manual-mirror trap this task's brief warned about — this pack caught it by checking the manual's own broadcast/addendum index, which shows no update newer than December 2021 (predating BBCE, OBBBA, and at least four COLA cycles), and used the manual only for one narrow, cross-corroborated structural feature (PFD Hold Harmless) rather than any dollar figure. AS 47.27.015's exact statutory text could not be fetched directly — law.justia.com and codes.findlaw.com both returned HTTP 403 to every direct curl attempt with a browser User-Agent — and was instead cross-corroborated across three independent secondary sources (FindLaw's own search-result excerpt, Justia's 2025-edition search-result excerpt, and CLASP's 50-state survey), all three of which quote materially identical statutory language, giving reasonable but not primary-fetch-level confidence.
